title: What Is the Real-Time Atomistic Mechanism Behind Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity in Donor-Chiral Bridge-Acceptor Molecules?
authors: Shu-Zheng Zhou, Xi Sun, Kai-Yuan Zhang, Hua-Hua Fu
abstract: Chiral-induced spin selectivity (CISS) has been experimentally observed in photo-excited donor-chiral bridge-acceptor (D-Bχ-A) molecules [Science 382, 197-201 (2023)]. However, the microscopic mechanism underlying CISS in such chiral systems remains elusive. Here we develop a quantum dynamical model that precisely maps the atomic structure of binaphthyl-type bridge dimers in isolated D-Bχ-A molecules and introduce a geometric spin-orbit coupling (SOC) mechanism to unveil the intrinsic origin of CISS in axially chiral systems. During photo-excited electron transport along the twisted pathways, the geometric SOC coupling strength exceeds the intrinsic coupling of light atoms by one to two orders of magnitude, readily producing observable high spin polarizations. The resulting spin polarization comprises two components: the CISS-associated polarizations along and perpendicular to the chiral axis are intrinsic to axial chirality, requiring neither external fields nor spin-superexchange transfer, while a non-Abelian curvature correction provides a rigorous mathematical definition of the chiral axis direction. Our calculated polarization components, chirality dependence, and relative magnitudes (30-40\%) quantitatively match time-resolved electron paramagnetic resonance measurements. This geometric SOC framework offers a self-consistent and general physical picture of CISS in axially chiral molecules and provides explicit theoretical guidance for the design of chiral spintronic devices.
summary: This paper reveals that the real-time spin polarization in chiral molecules like D-Bχ-A systems originates primarily from a geometric spin-orbit coupling ($	ext{SOC}_{	ext{geo}}$). By modeling electron transport along the molecule's twisted bridge, the authors show this mechanism generates strong, measurable spin polarizations that match experimental data. This provides a general theoretical blueprint for designing chiral spintronic devices.
main_problem: The primary goal is to elucidate the real-time, atomistic mechanism responsible for Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity (CISS) in Donor-Chiral Bridge-Acceptor (D-Bχ-A) molecules.
main_result: The study proposes that a geometric spin-orbit coupling ($	ext{SOC}_{	ext{geo}}$), arising from the curvature of electron transport along the chiral bridge, is the dominant mechanism generating observable high spin polarizations. This framework successfully accounts for both axial and transverse polarization components observed in experiments.
method: The authors developed and utilized a quantum dynamical model incorporating time-dependent charge-state populations and explicitly calculating geometric SOC derived from the Frenet–Serret frame along the twisted molecular pathway.
model_or_system: The system studied is the D-Bχ-A molecule, focusing on binaphthyl-type chiral bridge dimers. The theoretical framework involves deriving a Hamiltonian that includes $	ext{SOC}_{	ext{geo}}$ and analyzing spin dynamics using quantum master equations or density matrix propagation.
key_observables: Spin polarization components ($	ext{SP}_x, 	ext{SP}_y, 	ext{SP}_z$), the magnitude of geometric SOC (predicted to be $1-2$ orders of magnitude larger than intrinsic coupling), and population/coherence polarizations.
important_parameters: The relative magnitudes of polarization components ($\sim 30\%–40\%$ for CISS contribution) and the ratio $\lambda/t_0 \approx 0.64$ defining the SOC energy scale are key parameters.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the geometric SOC mechanism provides a self-consistent picture, allowing polarization to be understood without relying solely on conventional radical-pair mechanisms (RPM).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate molecular geometries and transport pathways, detailing how the geometric SOC is decomposed along orthogonal axes ($x, y, z$) across different enantiomers.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the mechanistic gap in CISS understanding. It then develops a quantum dynamical model incorporating $	ext{SOC}_{	ext{geo}}$ derived from molecular geometry (Frenet–Serret frame). Finally, it calculates and compares resulting spin polarization components against time-resolved electron paramagnetic resonance measurements.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly detailed, first-principles theoretical mechanism for CISS that moves beyond simple models. The explicit derivation of geometric SOC from molecular curvature is crucial for designing next-generation chiral spintronic materials.
